report.source_text: The patient was followed up in the clinic for six months postoperatively. He reported the resolution of his symptoms, and his blood pressure was normal on follow-up visits. Repeat imaging did not show any evidence of tumor recurrence.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 45-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of episodic headaches, palpitations, sweating, anxiety, and irritability, with elevated blood pressure (170/100 mmHg) on examination. Laboratory investigations revealed markedly elevated plasma catecholamines (epinephrine 550 pg/mL, norepinephrine 700 pg/mL) and metanephrines (metanephrine 1800 pg/mL, normetanephrine 1200 pg/mL), confirming catecholamine excess. Imaging studies (MRI and CT) identified a 3 cm mass in the left adrenal gland with local invasion into surrounding tissues. Histopathological examination of the surgical specimen confirmed pheochromocytoma, measuring 3.5 cm with capsular and vascular invasion, low mitotic rate (Ki-67 index 5%), and negative for malignancy markers. The patient underwent surgical resection. At six-month postoperative follow-up, he reported complete resolution of symptoms, normalization of blood pressure, and no evidence of tumor recurrence on repeat imaging.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Classic clinical presentation of catecholamine excess with episodic symptoms
Biochemical confirmation of elevated catecholamines and metanephrines
Imaging localization of adrenal tumor with invasion
Successful surgical treatment with complete symptom resolution and no recurrence

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Markedly elevated plasma catecholamines and metanephrines (E002) with imaging-confirmed adrenal mass (E003) and histopathological confirmation (E007) establish organic catecholamine-secreting tumor rather than functional disorder
Histopathology (E007) showed negative malignancy markers, low mitotic rate, and Ki-67 index of only 5%, with no recurrence at 6-month follow-up (E008)
